idiom_name: scope-exit hook + closure (defer/ensure/finally, RAII destructor, with/using declaration or registered exit callback)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: at the moment a resource or a piece of state is acquired, register the exit action with the runtime's scope-exit mechanism - a destructor, a defer/ensure/finally block, a with/using declaration, or a guard object holding a closure - so that every later way out of the scope (normal return, early return, exception or panic, break/continue, cancellation) runs the action exactly once, in reverse order of registration. Provide an explicit dismiss/release operation for commit semantics ('run the action unless committed') instead of arming the guard conditionally, and keep the action short, idempotent and non-throwing because it runs on failure paths where an error cannot be reported normally. What replaces the classic guard class is the hook itself; only where the language has no scope-exit hook must the action be attached to an owner object (RAII / Execute-Around) or written out at each exit path.
code_sketch:
acquire(resource)
guard = exit_hook(action = release(resource))   # runs at scope exit, all paths
... use(resource) ...                          # any early exit runs the action
commit()  ->  guard.dismiss()                  # opt out on the success path
pitfalls: The action runs while the scope's state is already invalid; a guard that reads locals being reconstructed or a resource being destroyed turns a clean failure into a second, confusing one.

An action that throws or aborts on the unwinding path either masks the original error (finally/ensure semantics, suppressed exceptions) or kills the process (double panic), so exit actions must be infallible.

A guard that is not reachable from the exit hook - bound to a temporary, shadowed by a loop iteration, dismissed by a move, or dismissed accidentally - fails silently rather than reporting that cleanup did not run.
Deferring cleanup inside an unbounded or long-lived loop retains every iteration's resource until the outer scope exits; introduce an inner scope or release explicitly at the iteration boundary.
Arming a release action before acquisition has succeeded can invoke cleanup on an invalid handle; initialize and validate the resource first, or make the guard conditional on successful acquisition.
Mixing scope-based cleanup with goto-based or manual teardown in one function can double-release or obscure ordering; choose one teardown mechanism for each resource and make handoff explicit.
